transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Good morning. Hinchingbrooke Country Park, Sally speaking. I'm one of the rangers.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: Oh hello. My name's John Chapman, and I'm a teaching assistant at a local primary school. I've been asked to arrange a visit to the park for two of our classes.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: OK. What would you like to know?

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: Well, I'm new to this area, so perhaps you could tell me something about the park first, please.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Of course. Altogether the park covers 170 acres, that's <q id="1">69 hectares</q>. There are three main types of habitat: wetland, grassland and woodland. The woods are well established and varied, with an oak plantation, and other areas of mixed species.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: The wetland is quite varied, too. The original farmland was dug up around 40 years ago to extract gravel. Once this work was completed, the gravel pits filled with water, forming the two large lakes. There are also several smaller ones, ponds and a <q id="2">stream</q> that flows through the park.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: OK, so I suppose with these different habitats there's quite a variety of wildlife.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: There certainly is – a lot of different species of birds and insects, and also animals like deer and rabbits.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: And I understand you organise educational visits for school parties.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: That's right. We can organise a wide range of activities and adapt them to suit all ages.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: Can you give me some examples of the activities?

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Well, one focus is on science, where we help children to discover and study plants, trees and insects. They also collect and analyse <q id="3">data</q> about the things they see.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: Uhuh.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Another focus is on geography. The park is a great environment to learn and practise reading a <q id="4">map</q> and using a compass to navigate around the park.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: Do you do anything connected with history?

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Yes, we do. For instance, the children can explore how the use of the land has changed over time. Then there's leisure and tourism.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: That focuses on your <q id="5">visitors</q>, I would imagine.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Yes, mostly. The children find out about them, their requirements, the problems they may cause and how we manage these. And another subject we cover is music: here the children experiment with natural materials to create <q id="6">sounds</q> and explore rhythm and tempo.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: That must be fun!

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Most children really enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: And of course, all the activities are educational, too. Learning outside the classroom encourages children to be creative, and to explore and discover for themselves.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: I would imagine they get a sense of <q id="7">freedom</q> that might not be a normal part of their lives.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: That's right. And very often the children discover that they can do things they didn't know they could do, and they develop new <q id="8">skills</q>. This gives them greater self-confidence.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: It sounds great. So, what about the practical side of it? How much does it cost for a full-day visit? We would expect to bring between 30 and 40 children.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: If there are over 30, it costs <q id="9">£4.95</q> for each child who attends on the day. We invoice you afterwards, so you don't pay for children who can't come because of sickness, for example. There's no charge for <q id="10">leaders</q> and other adults – as many as you want to bring.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: That sounds very fair. Well, thanks for all the information. I'll need to discuss it with my colleagues, and I hope to get back to you soon to make a booking.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: We'll look forward to hearing from you. Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: JOHN
transcript.text: Goodbye, and thank you.

It's great to see so many members of the Twinning Association here tonight. Since the twinning link between our two towns, Stanthorpe here in England and Malatte in France, was established, the relationship between the towns has gone from strength to strength.

Last month, 25 members of the association from Stanthorpe spent a weekend in Malatte. Our hosts had arranged a great programme. We learned how cheese is produced in the region and had the chance to taste the products. The theme park trip had to be cancelled, but we all had a great time on <q id="11">the final boat trip down the river – that was the real highlight</q>.

This is a special year for the Association because it's 25 years since we were founded. In Malatte, they're planning to mark this by building a footbridge in the municipal park. We've been discussing what to do here and <q id="12">we've decided to plant a poplar tree in the museum gardens</q>. We considered buying a garden seat to put there, but the authorities weren't happy with that idea.

In terms of fundraising to support our activities, we've done very well. <q id="13">Our pancake evening was well attended and made record profits</q>. And everyone enjoyed the demonstration of French cookery, which was nearly as successful. Numbers for our film show were limited because of the venue so we're looking for somewhere bigger next year.

We're looking forward to welcoming our French visitors here next week, and I know that many of you here will be hosting individuals or families. The coach from France will arrive at 5 pm on Friday. Don't try to do too much that first evening as they'll be tired, so <q id="14">have dinner in the house or garden rather than eating out</q>. The weather looks as if it'll be OK so you might like to plan a barbecue. Then the next morning's market day in town, and that's always a good place to stroll round.

On Saturday evening, we'll all meet up at the football club, where once again <q id="15">we'll have Toby Sharp and his band performing English and Scottish country songs</q>. Toby will already be well known to many of you as last year he organised our special quiz night and presented the prizes.

Now on Sunday, we'll be taking our visitors to Farley House. You may not all be familiar with it, so here's a map to help you. You can see the car park at the bottom of the map. There's an excellent farm shop in the grounds where our visitors can buy local produce – <q id="16">it's in the old stables, which is the first building you come to</q>. They're built round a courtyard, and the shop's <q id="16">in the far corner on the left</q>. There's also a small café on the right as you go in.

I know that one or two of our visitors may not be all that mobile. The main entrance to the house has a lot of steps so you might want to use the disabled entry. <q id="17">This is on the far side of the house from the car park</q>.

Children will probably be most interested in the adventure playground. <q id="18">That's at the northern end of the larger lake, in a bend on the path that leads to the lake</q>. There's lots for children to do there.

There are a number of lovely gardens near the house. <q id="19">The kitchen gardens are rectangular and surrounded by a wall</q>. They're to the north-east of the house, quite near the smaller lake. They're still in use and have a great collection of fruit and vegetables.

The Temple of the Four Winds is a bit more of a walk – but it's worth it. Take the path from the car park and go past the western sides of the stables and the house. Then <q id="20">when the path forks, take the right-hand path. Go up there with the woods on your left and the temple is right at the end</q>. There are great views over the whole area.
OK, so that's . . .

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: I haven't seen you for a bit, Marie.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: No. I've been busy with my project.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: You're making a vegan alternative to eggs, aren't you? Something that doesn't use animal products?

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: Yes. I'm using chickpeas. I had two main aims when I first started looking for an alternative to eggs, but actually I've found chickpeas have got more advantages.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: But how about your project on reusing waste food – you were looking at bread, weren't you?

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Yes. It's been hard work, but I've enjoyed it. The basic process was quite straightforward – breaking the stale bread down to a paste then reforming it.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: But you were using 3-D printing, weren't you, to make the paste into biscuits?

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd used that before, but in this project, <q id="21">I had time to play around with different patterns for the biscuits and finding how I could add fruit and vegetables to make them a more appetising colour, and I was really pleased with what I managed to produce</q>.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: <q id="22">It must've been a great feeling to make something appetising out of bits of old bread that would've been thrown away otherwise</q>.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: It was. And I'm hoping that some of the restaurants in town will be interested in the biscuits. I'm going to send them some samples.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: I came across something on the internet yesterday that might interest you. It was a company that's developed touch-sensitive sensors for food labels.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Mmm?

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: It's a special sort of label on the food package. When the label's smooth, the food is fresh and then when you can feel bumps on the label, that means the food's gone bad. It started off as a project to help visually impaired people know whether food was fit to eat or not.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Interesting. So just solid food?

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: No, things like milk and juice as well. But actually, <q id="23">I thought it might be really good for drug storage in hospitals and pharmacies</q>.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Right. And coming back to food, maybe it'd be possible to use it for other things besides freshness. Like <q id="24">how many kilograms a joint of meat is, for example</q>.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: Yes, there's all sorts of possibilities.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: I was reading an article about food trends predicting how eating habits might change in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: Oh – things like <q id="25">more focus on local products</q>? That seems so obvious, but the shops are still full of imported foods.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: <q id="25">Yes, they need to be more proactive to address that</q>.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: And somehow motivate consumers to change, yes.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: One thing everyone's aware of is <q id="26">the need for a reduction in unnecessary packaging</q> – but just about everything you buy in supermarkets is still covered in plastic. The government needs to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: <q id="26">Absolutely. It's got to change</q>.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Do you think there'll be more interest in gluten- and lactose-free food?

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: For people with allergies or food intolerances? I don't know. <q id="27">Lots of people I know have been buying that type of food for years now</q>.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: <q id="27">Yes, even if they haven't been diagnosed with an allergy</q>.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: That's right. One thing I've noticed is the number of branded products related to celebrity chefs – people watch them cooking on TV and then buy things like spice mixes or frozen foods with the chef's name on . . . <q id="28">I bought something like that once, but I won't again</q>.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: <q id="28">Yeah – I bought a ready-made spice mix for chicken which was supposed to be used by a chef I'd seen on television, and it didn't actually taste of anything</q>.

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: Mm. Did the article mention 'ghost kitchens' used to produce takeaway food?

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: No. What are they?

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: Well, they might have the name of a restaurant, but actually they're a cooking facility just for delivery meals – the public don't ever go there. But <q id="29">people aren't aware of that – it's all kept very quiet</q>.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: <q id="29">So people don't realise the food's not actually from the restaurant</q>?

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Did you know more and more people are using all sorts of different mushrooms now, to treat different health concerns? Things like heart problems?

transcript.speaker: MARIE
transcript.text: Hmm. <q id="30">They might be taking a big risk there</q>.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: <q id="30">Yes, it's hard to know which varieties are safe to eat</q>.

transcript.speaker: COLIN
transcript.text: Anyway maybe now . . .

For my presentation today, I'm going to talk about the Céide Fields in the northwest of Ireland, one of the largest Neolithic sites in the world. I recently visited this site and observed the work that is currently being done by a team of archaeologists there.

The site was first discovered in the 1930s by a local teacher, Patrick Caulfield. He noticed that when local people were digging in the bog, they were constantly hitting against what seemed to be <q id="31">rows of stones. He realised that these must be walls</q> and that they must be thousands of years old for them to predate the bog which subsequently grew over them.

He wrote to the National Museum in Dublin to ask them to investigate, but no one took him seriously. It wasn't until 40 years later, when <q id="32">Patrick Caulfield's son Seamus, who had become an archaeologist</q> by then, began to explore further. He inserted iron probes into the bog to map the formation of the stones, <q id="33">a traditional method which local people had always used for finding fuel</q> buried in the bog for thousands of years. Carbon dating later proved that the site was over 5,000 years old and was the largest Neolithic site in Ireland.

Thanks to the bog which covers the area, the remains of the settlement at Céide Fields, which is over 5,000 years old, are extremely well-preserved. A bog is 90 percent water; its soil is so saturated that when the grasses and heathers that grow on its surface die, they don't fully decay but accumulate in layers. <q id="34">Objects remain so well preserved in these conditions because of the acidity of the peat and the deficiency of oxygen</q>. At least 175 days of rain a year are required for this to happen; this part of Ireland gets an average of 225 days.

The Neolithic farmers at Céide would have enjoyed several centuries of relative peace and stability. Neolithic farmers generally lived in larger communities than their predecessors, with a number of houses built around a community building. As they lived in permanent settlements, Neolithic farmers were able to build bigger <q id="35">houses. These weren't round as people often assume, but rectangular</q> with a small hole in the roof that allowed smoke to escape. This is one of many innovations and indicates that the Neolithic farmers were the first people to cook indoors. Another new technology that Neolithic settlers brought to Ireland was pottery. Fragments of Neolithic pots have been found in Céide and elsewhere in Ireland. The pots were used for many things; as well as for storing food, pots were filled with a small amount of fat and when this was set alight, <q id="36">they served as lamps</q>.

It's thought that the Céide Fields were mainly used as paddocks for animals to graze in. Evidence from the Céide Fields suggests that <q id="37">each plot of land was of a suitable size to sustain an extended family</q>. They may have used a system of rotational grazing in order to prevent over-grazing and to allow for plant recovery and regrowth. This must have been a year-round activity as <q id="38">no structures have been found which would have been used to shelter animals in the winter</q>.

However, archaeologists believe that this way of life at Céide ceased abruptly. Why was this? Well, several factors may have contributed to the changing circumstances. <q id="39">The soil would have become less productive</q> and led to the abandonment of farming. The crop rotation system was partly responsible for this as it would have been very intensive and was not sustainable. But there were also climatic pressures too. The farmers at Céide would have enjoyed a relatively dry period, but this began to change and the conditions became wetter as <q id="40">there was a lot more rain</q>. It was these conditions that encouraged the bog to form over the area which survives today.
So now I'd like to show you some . . .
